evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing the received Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s commentary
evidence.field: 咳 entry; graphic and lexical account
evidence.text: The received entry defines 咳 as “a young child’s laugh,” analyzes it as 口 plus phonetic 亥, and records 孩 as its old-form spelling with 子 in place of 口. Duan Yucai notes that Liji · Neize and Mengzi write this word with 孩. This supports an old graphic spelling relation between 孩 and 咳, but does not establish whether the separate child-noun 孩 arose by semantic extension from “laugh” or was an independent word using the same graph.
evidence.title: 說文解字「咳」

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Republic of China, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 孩 entry; orthographic status and cited usages
evidence.text: The dictionary says 孩 is not separately entered in Shuowen, cites the Shuowen statement under 咳 that 孩 is the old form of 咳 written with 子, and distinguishes the child-laugh reading from the noun meaning infant or young child. It cites Liji · Neize’s “孩而名之,” Mengzi’s “孩提之童,” Li Mi’s Jin-era “生孩六月,” and Liji · Yue Ling’s “孩蟲.” This documents multiple senses and citations but supplies no palaeographic sequence for 孩.
evidence.title: A00995 孩 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database reports no displayed oracle-bone, bronze, seal, or bamboo-slip forms for 孩 in its entry; its cited Shuowen material is 咳, with 孩 as the old spelling. It analyzes the later compound as 子 semantic plus 亥 phonetic and glosses 孩 primarily as infant/young child. It cites Guangyun, compiled in 1008, “始生小兒” (newborn/very young child); Jin poet Guo Pu and Li Mi’s 3rd-century memorial for infant uses; Liji · Yue Ling for “young” in 孩蟲; and the old child-laugh use as another sense. Lack of displayed early forms in this database is not proof that none exist.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 孩

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Songben Guangyun entry as indexed in search results
evidence.text: The Guangyun entry glosses 孩 as “始生小兒” (newly born or very young child) and gives 戶來切. The available page search result identifies it as Songben Guangyun, page 100, entry 49; opening the CText page failed, so this was not independently inspected beyond the returned result.
evidence.title: 廣韻: 上平聲: 咍: 孩

evidence.text: Shuowen’s Han-dynasty account describes 子 through the seasonal theory of the eleventh month and says the graph is pictographic. This is a historical lexicographic explanation, not direct confirmation of its original pictorial interpretation.
evidence.title: 說文解字/14

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 子; graphic history and early uses
evidence.text: The database describes 子 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as a depiction of an infant, including forms emphasizing the large head and moving arms. It reports that the graph was used for children and also borrowed for the first earthly branch; another early graph was used for the sixth branch, later represented by 巳. This independently supports 子’s semantic suitability as the meaning element in 孩.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 子

evidence.text: The database lists oracle-bone and bronze exemplars for 子 and describes it as a pictograph for an infant, with the arms’ movement emphasized. The record establishes early forms for the component 子, not an early form of the compound 孩.
evidence.title: 漢字「子」：字形演變

evidence.text: Shuowen glosses 亥 as 荄 and associates its form with the seasonal cycle, male and female, and a pregnant child’s sounds; it also records an old form said to be 豕. These are received Han-dynasty explanations, not settled modern accounts of the graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 說文解字/14

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database says the oracle-bone and bronze form’s original meaning is unresolved. One proposal, associated with Xu Shen and later scholars, sees buried plant roots and links 亥 to 荄; another proposal treats it as pig-like or historically identical with 豕. The database notes that close comparison with oracle-bone 豕 forms weakens the root and pig accounts and concludes that no satisfactory explanation is established. It separately reports the established later use of 亥 as the twelfth earthly branch and its zodiac association with pig. This uncertainty concerns 亥’s referent, not its later phonetic use in compounds.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 亥

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 亥 entry, quoting Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014) reconstruction tables
evidence.text: Modern Standard Mandarin Pinyin is hài; Standard Guangzhou–Hong Kong Cantonese Jyutping is hoi⁶. Middle Chinese is given as Baxter hojX, corresponding to Guangyun 胡改切. Old Chinese reconstructions are Zhengzhang *ɡɯːʔ and Baxter–Sagart *[ɡ]ˤəʔ. These system-specific reconstructions support a close sound relationship to 孩’s reconstructed Old Chinese; they do not identify the original depicted object’s spoken name.
evidence.title: 亥 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 孩 entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014) reconstruction tables
evidence.text: The page classifies 孩 as a phonosemantic compound, semantic 子 plus phonetic 亥. It gives Mandarin Pinyin hái and Cantonese Jyutping haai⁴, with dated hoi⁴ also recorded. It gives Middle Chinese Baxter hoj and Old Chinese Zhengzhang *ɡɯː versus Baxter–Sagart *[ɡ]ˤə. Compared with 亥, Zhengzhang has the same onset and rhyme with a final glottal stop on 亥; Baxter–Sagart likewise differs principally in the 亥 final glottal stop. This is strong independent phonological support for 亥’s phonetic role. Modern sound similarity alone is not the basis for the classification.
evidence.title: 孩 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 子 entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014) tables
evidence.field: 子; pronunciation comparison for semantic component assessment
evidence.text: Mandarin Pinyin is zǐ; Middle Chinese Baxter is tsiX. Old Chinese is Zhengzhang *ʔslɯʔ and Baxter–Sagart *[ts]əʔ / *tsəʔ, depending on the listed reading. This pronunciation is unlike 孩’s reconstructed *ɡɯː, consistent with 子 serving semantically rather than as the sound element in 孩. The table contains separate 子 readings, so the form distinction should not be mistaken for a statement that every use of 子 had one pronunciation.
evidence.title: 子 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The page lists 孩 and 亥 in the 亥 phonetic series with Zhengzhang Old Chinese *ɡɯː and *ɡɯːʔ respectively, and lists them alongside a broader series including 荄, 骸, and 核. This supports sound-series classification; it does not by itself establish that the words share a semantic origin or that 孩 meant “to sprout.”
evidence.title: 亥 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: Smith groups 孩 with 荄, 根, 核, 骸, and 亥 in a proposed family with meanings around root, germ, or generative core, and suggests a derivation from 荄 to a proposed verb 孩 “sprout” by voicing. The cited account itself says this derivation is not further explained and that “to sprout” for 孩 is not attested. This is a disputed etymological proposal, distinct from the well-supported graphic phonetic role of 亥 in 孩.
evidence.title: 亥 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 咳; lexical senses and cross-spelling evidence
evidence.text: The specialist entry distinguishes 咳 meaning a baby’s laugh from the child noun and notes that the latter was written with 孩 in sources including Shiji · Bian Que biography. It cites the pre-imperial Liji · Neize wording “咳而名之” for the laugh-related use, and a Western Han Mawangdui Laozi silk manuscript, dated 2nd century BCE, with “若嬰兒未咳.” It also warns that the later cough sense of 咳 is a homograph and semantically unrelated. Thus attestations of the child-laugh word should not be conflated with later cough or with all child-noun uses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 咳

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 孩; attestation sequence and semantic extension limits
evidence.text: The database cites 孩蟲 in Liji · Yue Ling for “young/immature” creatures, and cites “孩提之童” in Mengzi · Jinxin I, whose traditional Zhao Qi commentary explains a child old enough to laugh and be carried. It also records the Jin-era Li Mi phrase “生孩六月.” These citations document laugh, infant/young child, and young/immature senses in separate textual contexts. They do not establish a single dated semantic chain from laughing to child to immature.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 孩

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 孩 entry; Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants; Academia Sinica database
evidence.text: Modern Standard Mandarin: hái (Pinyin); Standard Guangzhou–Hong Kong Cantonese: haai⁴ (Jyutping), with dated hoi⁴; Korean Hanja: hae, Hangul 해; Japanese Go-on がい (gai), Kan-on かい (kai), kun ちのみご (chinomigo); Vietnamese Hán Nôm readings include hài. These are modern or later reading traditions, not evidence for the character’s origin. The Japanese kun reading is a native gloss/read word, not a Japanese-created character claim.
evidence.title: 孩 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, International Character and Variant Knowledge Base
evidence.field: 孩; database scope for palaeographic forms
evidence.text: The inspected entry gives modern character metadata, readings and senses but provides no textual account or displayed early graph sequence for 孩 in its accessible text. It lists infant laugh, child/young child, young/immature, affection/treat as a baby, surname, and variant of 咳. The database’s lack of accessible glyph records here is a coverage gap, not proof that the character is absent from all ancient manuscripts or inscriptions.
evidence.title: 漢字「孩」：基本資料

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Smith (2011) and Zhengzhang sound tables
evidence.field: 亥; graphic changes and possible corruption
evidence.text: The sources inspected show divergent accounts for the original 亥 graph, including plant root and pig-like explanations, plus a reported historical confusion between 亥 and 豕 in textual transmission. The idiom 鲁鱼亥豕 reflects graphic copying confusion; it is not evidence that the two graphs had the same origin. No inspected source established corruption as the origin of the 亥 component in 孩. For 孩 itself, accessible sources document the received old spelling under 咳 and later regular left-right form, but did not provide a dated sequence of its own early glyphs.
evidence.title: 亥 — Wiktionary

gaps: No inspected source provides a dated oracle-bone, bronze, or early manuscript form of the compound 孩 itself; do not infer a chronological glyph sequence from component histories.

No direct evidence establishes when the child noun 孩 separated from or became associated with the Shuowen-listed old spelling of the baby-laugh word 咳. The observed senses may represent extension, parallel lexical use, or some combination.

The original depicted referent and pronunciation of 亥 remain unsettled. The strong phonetic comparison is between independently reconstructed character readings 孩 and 亥, not a recovered name for 亥’s pictured object.
Smith’s proposed semantic family and derivation of 孩 as “sprout” are not independently demonstrated by the inspected evidence; the “sprout” sense is unattested in the source’s own summary.
CText source pages intermittently failed to open (one 403 and two internal fetch errors). Search-result snippets were not treated as inspected primary pages.
The Han-period Shuowen account is preserved as lexicographic testimony; it does not by itself establish original formation chronology or settle the graphic origins of 亥.
